title: Inputs You Did Not Think Of: Properties, Generators and Shrinking

questions.question: Nine careful examples are written for a parser: empty, non-numeric, trailing rubbish, leading zeros, a large round number. The parser has no overflow check. How many of the nine fail?
options: None: the person who thinks of the cases is the person who wrote the code
One, the large round number
Two, the empty string and the large number
All of the numeric ones
questions.explanation: The value that catches it is 18446744073709551616, which is not exotic. It is simply longer than anybody types into a test by hand. Generated inputs found it in 1.6 values on average.

questions.question: Which property catches a parser that silently wraps a too-large number?
options: That an accepted value prints back as the text it was given, once leading zeros are discounted
That the value survives being printed and read again
That the value is less than the maximum of the type
That parsing the same text twice gives the same answer
questions.explanation: The round trip through the value is true even when the parser has wrapped, because the wrapped value is a perfectly good number and round trips as itself. Choosing the property is most of the work.

questions.question: Three generators hunt the same fault. One over any printable byte finds it in 0 of 20 seeds; one over digits up to forty finds it in all 20; one over digits up to ten finds it in 0. What is the difference between the two that failed?
options: The wide one will not reach it in any run you have time for; the narrow one cannot reach it at all, at any number of trials
Nothing: both simply need more trials
The wide one is testing the wrong function
The narrow one is too slow to run enough values
questions.explanation: The largest number nine digits can spell is nowhere near the largest the parser can hold. That generator would report the parser correct for ever, on any machine. From the outside both look the same: a green tick and a large trial count.

questions.question: A property has never failed. How do you find out whether it can?
options: Break the code on purpose and watch it fail, the same discipline as any other test
Increase the number of trials until it does
Compare its coverage against the example tests
Check that the generator is uniformly distributed
questions.explanation: A property written carelessly can be satisfied by the code doing nothing. The tell is that it passes on the broken version and the fixed one: it does not change when the code does.

questions.question: A generated test fails on the build server. What must the report contain for it to be evidence?
options: The seed, so the same values can be asked for again
The full list of values tried
The line number of the failure
The number of trials before it failed
questions.explanation: A generator seeded from the clock finds a bug, prints a failure and takes the evidence with it. That is worse than no test, because it teaches people the suite is flaky.

questions.question: Failures from the aimed generator averaged 29.17 characters. After shrinking they were all exactly 20. What is the one thing a shrinker must never do?
options: Return a value that passes: everything it hands back has to have failed on the way
Change the length of the input
Take more than a few steps
Return a value the generator could not have produced
questions.explanation: Twenty digits is the shortest number that parser gets wrong, and the shrinker finds that without being told. A shrunk counterexample is usually enough to see the bug without a debugger.
